messages.subject: degrees of freedom
parts:
Hi all!
I would like to know what's the difference between the effective degrees of freedom and the reference degrees of freedom that appears in the output of a dsm model.
Thank you very much in advance!

Antonella

messages.author: 350dad0a615d36db
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] degrees of freedom
parts:
Hi Antonella, hi listfolk,

This is a good question and one that has a bit of a technical answer.

The models fitted by dsm are just GAMs, as fitted by mgcv. So, anything
that applies to mgcv models also applies to dsm. A (somewhat technical)
answer is in ?summary.gam, which describes (at least some of) the output
in the summary table for dsm too.

A quick explanation:

You set a maximum degrees of freedom (sometimes called complexity or
basis size) when you setup a smooth in your model. This is done using
the k=... parameter in s() or te(). The value is set automatically if
you don't supply it (see ?choose.k for more information on how to set
k). This parameter sets the absolute limit on how wiggly the model will be.

During model fitting, we don't use all of those degrees of freedom
(usually), as the penalty reduces the wigglyness to be the "right"
amount. This gives us the EDF, the effective degrees of freedom for that
term. This is how wiggly the model things that term should be.

If we want to do a significance test and ask "should we have this term
in the model?" (equivalently "should this term be 0?"), we need to have
some degrees of freedom for that test. So we could use k, above, to do
that. This is fine but often we set k too large because we don't know
how wiggly the true smooth is and we want to make sure that there is
enough flexibility in the smooth from the outset. If we use the k in
that case, we might end up with (non)significant effects when really it
was just because we set k to big. For that reason we set a reference
degrees of freedom to use for the tests (that gives us the p-values at
the end of each line).

The technical side of this is covered in this paper:
https://academic.oup.com/biomet/article-abstract/100/1/221/192816?redirectedFrom=fulltext


Short answer: ref.df is the degrees of freedom that will be used for the
tests to see if the smooths are significant.


Hope this helps!

cheers,
--dave
